episode.title: Morning Drops #43 - Looking Back
episode.description:
In this first Morning Drop of 2026, Yasmin opens a space for quiet reflection on the nature of transitions. The episode traces a personal journey that began three years ago, when a sudden injury on New Year’s Day turned a desire for movement into a mandatory season of stillness.

Through the story of a broken knee and the slow process of relearning to walk, the narrative explores the difference between being strong and being aware. It touches on the vulnerability of the body, the unexpected joy found in daily progress, and the warmth that comes from finally allowing oneself to accept help. The musical selection mirrors this path of recovery, moving from the uncertainty of change to the steady rhythm of healing.

The broadcast blended ceremonial pageantry with pop culture, foreshadowing the monarchy’s shift into a kind of live, ongoing media spectacle.

queue.fact_text: In 1948, Czechoslovak president Edvard Beneš chose to resign rather than sign the Ninth-of-May Constitution, which would have cemented full Communist control. His quiet refusal, made in poor health, became a symbolic last stand for the pre-war democratic republic as the country slipped behind the Iron Curtain.

queue.fact_text: At the Battle of Messines in 1917, Allied engineers spent months secretly digging tunnels under German lines and packing them with nearly a million pounds of explosives. When they detonated the mines just before dawn on June 7, the blasts were so vast that they were reportedly heard in London, about 200 kilometers away.

queue.fact_text: The 1862 Lyons–Seward Treaty between the United States and the United Kingdom quietly tightened the noose on the transatlantic slave trade by allowing British ships to search suspected slave vessels flying the U.S. flag. It was one of those diplomatic documents where a few lines of legal text helped close a brutal, centuries-long business.

episode.title: Morning Drops #24 - The Rise Of Afrobeat

queue.fact_text: In 1810, the Gazeta de Buenos Ayres became one of the first newspapers of the emerging Argentine nation, serving as both news outlet and revolutionary megaphone. Its editors used it to spread ideas of independence and identity, turning printed pages into tools for reshaping how a whole region saw itself.

episode.title: Morning Drops #52- Think Again
episode.description:

Along the way, we meet a Serbian trumpet player who had to let go of one dream to find another, a Tunisian oud master who challenged centuries of tradition from the inside, and a Japanese band who found freedom in playing for no one. The music moves from Balkan brass to Mediterranean stillness to psychedelic drift, tracing the shape of a mind opening up.

Listen slowly, and ask yourself: is there something you believe today that deserves a second look?

queue.fact_text: Explorer and surveyor David Thompson reached the mouth of the Saskatchewan River in 1800 after years of charting vast swathes of western Canada, often guided by Indigenous knowledge. queue.fact_text: The BBC’s 1946 return to TV wasn’t just technical—staff reportedly rehearsed how to speak to a population that hadn’t seen television in seven years. queue.fact_text: When Sony launched Betamax in 1975, they imagined people mostly using it to time-shift TV shows—not to build home movie libraries or rental empires. Yet that small idea of recording “what you missed” opened the door to binge-watching, pausing, and re-watching culture long before streaming existed.

published.fact_text: When Sony launched the Betamax format in 1975, home video recording was so new that early ads had to explain why anyone would want to tape a TV show. Betamax tapes were actually higher quality than their later VHS rivals, but Sony’s decision to keep the format more closed helped doom it in the famous “videotape format war.”

published.fact_text: In just about three minutes on June 7, 1692, an earthquake and tsunami caused parts of the pirate haven of Port Royal, Jamaica, to literally slide into the sea.
